title: Game 5: Magnus vs Hans
notes: Game 5 of 12 in the experiment, from the Sicilian Defence, Najdorf. Magnus (the learner) reads his notebook and similar past mistakes before every move; Hans (the control) has neither.

This is the Najdorf; the greedy Bxa6 loses a piece to ...Nxa6 (rule 2: count the recaptures), so I develop soundly. Be3 is the English Attack main line: it develops with no loose pieces, supports the d4 knight, and prepares f3, Qd2 and g4 with a healthy space edge.

This is the Najdorf English Attack, and I want to grab central space before White sets up f3/g4 plans. 6...e5 hits the knight — after 7.Nb3 (or Nf3) I follow with Be6 and Be7, and 7.Nf5?! Bxf5 8.exf5 d5 is fine for me. I checked 6...Nxe4 is bad because 7.Nxe4 d5 8.Bb5+ wins material.

Black's ...e5 hits my d4 knight, so I must move it; Nf5 can be met by ...g6 chasing it with no pawn support (rule 5), and Nb5/Ne6/Nc6 drop material to ...axb5 or ...fxe6. Nb3 is the main-line retreat: the knight is safe, keeps the c5/d4 squares covered, and leaves my e3 bishop and e4 pawn defensible.
This is the standard Najdorf English Attack structure; 7...Nxe4 just loses a piece to Nxe4, so I follow main theory. Be6 develops, covers d5 and c4, and prepares Be7/0-0 or Nbd7 with b5 play.

Qxd6 is a trap — the f8 bishop simply takes my queen, and 8.Nd5 Nxd5 9.exd5 Bxd5 just drops a pawn since nothing recaptures on d5. The solid main-line 8.f3 reinforces e4, takes the g4 square from his knight, and prepares Qd2 with castling, leaving no piece of mine loose.

White's slow 8.f3 neglects the center, so I strike immediately with 8...d5; after 9.exd5 Nxd5 10.Nxd5 Bxd5 the queens can come off on d5 and my pieces are active with no weaknesses. Nxe4 fails simply to fxe4, so the clean central break is best.

This is the main-line Najdorf/English Attack structure, and the standard answer to 8...d5 is 9.exd5, after which 9...Nxd5 10.Nxd5 Bxd5 (or 10...Qxd5 11.Qxd5 Bxd5) leaves me a healthy position with pressure on d5 and no loose pieces. I checked the alternatives: 9.Nxd5 Nxd5 10.exd5 Bxd5 surrenders the centre, and 9.Bxa6? bxa6 just gives away a bishop for a pawn while leaving d5 strong, so the capture count favours exd5.

9...Nxd5 is the natural recapture, developing pressure and inviting mass trades on d5 (10.Nxd5 Bxd5 11.Qxd5 Qxd5), after which my structure is sound and the e5 pawn is well supported. Recapturing with the bishop instead would leave my knight passive and allow White to keep more pieces, while Qxd5 invites tempo gains against the queen.

Bc4 fails tactically to 10...Nxe3 since the knight then forks my queen on d1, and Bb5+ simply drops a piece to axb5, so I take the centralised knight: 10.Nxd5 Bxd5 (or Qxd5) is an even trade where d5 is defended twice but I'm only swapping knight for knight. This removes Black's active piece, leaves my Be3 unattacked, and keeps a safe grip on the light squares with c4/Nc5 ideas to follow.

I need to recapture on d5; Qxd5 invites Bc4 harassing my queen, while Bxd5 is the solid Sicilian recapture that either trades queens after Qxd5 Qxd5 or leaves me a comfortable game with the dark-squared bishop and no weaknesses. I'll take with the bishop.

Black's bishop on d5 is his best piece, so I play Bc4 to offer a trade; c4 is only attacked by the d5 bishop, and after Bxc4 Nxc4 my knight recaptures and hits e5, while Be6 Bxe6 fxe6 wrecks his pawns. I checked the only tricky reply 11...Qa5+, which I meet with Qd2 or Bd2 and remain comfortable, and nothing of mine is left loose.

My bishop on d5 is awkward since White threatens Bxd5 (and Be4/Bxf3 both lose a piece to fxe4 or Qxf3), so I simplify with Bxc4; after Nxc4 my e5 pawn is attacked once and I'll meet that with Nc6 or Qc7, reaching a comfortable, roughly equal structure. The alternative Bb4+ 12.c3 Be7 runs into 13.Bxd5 when recapturing with the queen drops it to Qxd5, so trading on c4 myself is cleanest.

No piece of mine can legally capture on c4 (b3 is my own knight, and Qd3/Qd4/Qd5/Qe2 all simply lose the queen to Bxd3/exd4/Bxd5/Bxe2), so instead I develop with Nd2, which attacks the c4 bishop and gains the tempo back; Bxa2 fails to Rxa2 since my rook guards a2, and if the bishop goes to d5 I hit it again with c4. If Black tries Qh4+ I answer g3 and then collect or chase the bishop.

My bishop on c4 is attacked by the knight, and grabbing a2 loses the piece to b3 and Rxb1, while Bd5 just invites c4 with tempo. I retreat to e6 where the bishop is safe, keeps my bishop pair, and I can follow with Nc6, Be7 and castling.

I'm already a piece down after the Bc4 blunder, so I need safety and no further material loss: Nc4 loses the knight to Bxc4 (c4 is undefended), Bc5 loses the bishop to Bxc5, and Ne4 just gets chased by ...f5 with no pawn support. Castling tucks the king away, connects my rooks, and leaves nothing loose for Black to hit.

I have the bishop pair and a solid pawn structure, so I just need to finish development; Bxa2 loses to Rxa2 since the rook already eyes that square. Nc6 develops with tempo-free support of e5 and prepares Be7 and castling.

My first instinct Nc4 (hitting e5) loses a piece outright to ...Bxc4 since nothing recaptures on c4 — exactly the capture-count rule I keep breaking. Instead Ne4 puts the knight on a central square backed by the f3 pawn, controls d6/f6/c5/g5 against Black's uncastled king, and nothing attacks it right now; if ...f5 kicks it, Ng5 hits the e6 bishop.

I need to develop and castle; e5 is currently safe and White's knight on e4 has no good entry squares since Nd6+ or Nc5 just invites favorable exchanges for me. Grabbing a2 fails immediately to Rxa2, so I'll play the solid developing move and prepare to castle.

Ng5 and Nf6+ lose material (Bxg5 Bxg5 Qxg5; gxf6), and Qd5 just drops the queen to Bxd5, so I checked every destination for recapturers first. My loose pieces are Be3 and Ne4, so Qd3 fixes both at once (it also makes ...Bc5 a blunder since c5 is undefended), keeps the d-file pressure against the uncastled king and prepares Rfd1 or f4.

Bxa2 looks greedy but loses a piece to Ra1 (b1 and b3 are both covered), so I'll just complete development safely. Castling leaves nothing hanging — Nf6+ is answered by Bxf6, and Qxd8 only trades into an equal endgame where my two bishops are comfortable.

I checked every active try and most lose material to Black's bishop on e6: Qc4 and Qd5 run straight into Bxc4/Bxd5, Qxa6 drops to Rxa6 (a8 rook covers a6 through a7), and Nc5 is met by Bxc5 since the e7 bishop guards it. Rather than loosen anything, I bring the last piece into play with Rad1, taking the open d-file, keeping Ne4 defended by the queen and nothing of mine attacked.

Bxa2 loses the bishop after b3 and Rd1-a1 traps it, and Nd4 drops a pawn to Bxd4 exd4 Rxd4; so I want a solid developing move. Qc7 connects the rooks, defends b7 and e5, and takes the sting out of Ne4-c5 while preparing Rfd8 to contest the d-file.

Nc5 hits both b7 and the Be6, and the only capture of c5 is ...Bxc5, after which Bxc5 recaptures with a healthy active bishop hitting f8, so the recapture count favours me; if Black defends with ...b6 then Nxe6 fxe6 leaves him with a shattered structure and me with bishop versus knight. I checked that nothing in Black's camp hits my loose Be3 or creates a double attack after this move.

I'm already a full piece up (White dropped the bishop with 11.Bc4 Bxc4), so simplifying is the cleanest path — Bxc5 removes the annoying knight that eyes e6 and b7. After Bxc5 Bxc5 I keep bishop plus knight against a lone bishop with no tactics against me, whereas keeping the bishop pair with Bd5 invites c4 harassment.

Black has just taken my knight on c5, so I must recapture; I checked that c5 is covered by nothing black — Qc7's file is blocked by its own knight on c6, there's no b6 pawn, and Nc6 doesn't reach c5 — so Bxc5 is a clean recapture restoring material equality while trading toward a safe position. Alternatives like Qxh7+ lose the queen to Kxh7, and any other move simply leaves me a piece down.

Counting material, I'm a full piece up (White dropped a bishop back on move 11), so my priority is to simplify and avoid tactics — and right now my f8 rook is hanging to Bc5. Rfd8 saves the rook, is defended twice (Ra8 and Qc7), and invites rook trades down the d-file; lines like 19.Bd6 Rxd6 or 19.Qxd8+ Rxd8 20.Rxd8+ only leave me even further ahead.

I'm down a knight for a pawn, so I need a forcing resource: Bd6 hits the queen while being doubly defended by Qd3 and Rd1, so every capture sequence on d6 (Rxd6 Qxd6 Qxd6 Rxd6, or Qxd6 Qxd6 Rxd6 Rxd6) nets me rook-for-bishop and levels the material at two rooks versus rook, knight and bishop with an active rook. I rejected Qxd8+ because after Rxd8 the d8 square is covered by Qc7, so I'd just be giving queen for rook, and Qxa6/Qxh7+ lose the queen outright to Rxa6/Kxh7.

I'm a full piece up (White's bishop went for nothing earlier), so I must avoid the simplification 19...Qxd6 20.Qxd6 Rxd6 21.Rxd6, which trades my extra piece down to R+N+B vs two rooks. Instead Qb6+ moves the queen off the bishop's diagonal with tempo: Bc5 as a block just loses to Qxc5+, so White must play Kh1 or Rf2, and then b2 is hanging while his bishop on d6 is awkward (any bishop retreat opens the d-file for Rxd3, winning queen for rook).

I must answer the check on b6, and the interposing moves all fail — Qe3 and Bc5 drop a piece outright to Qxe3/Qxc5, and Qd4 is met by Nxd4 winning my queen for a knight; Rf2 is safe (king defends it) but passive, so I simply sidestep with Kh1, which leaves Bd6 solidly backed by Rd1 (Rxd6 Rxd6 just loses rook for bishop) and keeps all my pieces active. If Black grabs b2 I answer Rb1 and hit b7 with tempo.

The b2 pawn is simply hanging, and after 21.Rb1 Qxc2 22.Qxc2 there is no recapture, leaving me a pawn (or two) up. I also checked 21.Bxe5 Nxe5 22.Qxd8+ Rxd8 23.Rxd8+ Kh7, which leaves me with queen, knight and bishop against two rooks — clearly better for me, so the grab is safe.

Every bishop retreat or queen move off d3 is out because Rd8xd3 or Rxd6 tactics rely on Qd3+Rd1 both guarding d6, and Bxe5 loses the queen to ...Rxd3; instead Rb1 hits the undefended Qb2 with tempo while b1 is covered by Rf1 (Qxb1 Rxb1) and Qd3 still guards both c2 and the bishop on d6. I'm down material, so I want active rook play against b7 rather than trading into a dead-lost endgame.

I'm up a full bishop from White's earlier blunder, so my priority is to save my queen from Rb1 while simplifying; Qd4 both escapes and attacks White's queen (defended only by the c2 pawn), offering a trade that leaves me cleanly a piece ahead. If White tries Bxe5 hitting my queen, Nxe5 removes the attacker and hits Qd3, and Rxd6/Qxd3 resources keep everything covered.

Checking every defender of my destination squares saved me: the natural 22.Bc5 (hitting the queen) actually drops the bishop to 22...Qxc5, and leaving the bishop on d6 loses a piece to 22...Qxd6! Qxd6 Rxd6 since Rd8 stacks behind the queen. Bc7 is the one retreat no black unit covers (Rd8, Nc6, b7 and Be6 all miss it), and it counterattacks the d8 rook, so if Black trades queens with Qxd3 cxd3 I pick up Bxd8 Rxd8 — rook for bishop — which is my best practical chance while material down.

I'm a full piece and a pawn up, so I just need to consolidate safely: Rd7 attacks the undefended bishop on c7, defends b7 against Rxb7, and keeps a rook able to recapture on d4, so 23.Bxe5 Nxe5 24.Qxd4 Rxd4 no longer works for White. The bishop has almost no safe squares (b8 and a5 and d6 and f4 all lose material), so I win it or force a miserable retreat to b6.

I checked every retreat and my bishop on c7 is completely trapped — b8 and d8 fall to Ra8, d6 to Rd7, a5 to Nc6, and b6 to Qd4 — and no piece of mine can defend c7, so the bishop is lost whatever I do. Therefore I should at least take something with it: Bxe5 grabs a pawn and simultaneously hits the Qd4, and after Nxe5 (or Qxe5) I am only down a piece for two pawns instead of a piece for nothing.

I'm already up a piece, and White's bishop on e5 is only defended by the queen — but my own queen on d4 blocks the d-file, so Nxe5 is safe (Qxe5 instead would allow Qxd7). After Nxe5 Qxd4 Rxd4 I'm cleanly a knight and bishop ahead with no counterplay for White.

I'm down two pieces for a pawn, so my only practical hope is to kill Black's attacking potential — her queen on d4 combines with Ne5/Be6 against f3, g2 and h2 (…Nxf3! ideas), and grabbing a6 would let that storm start. Trading queens with 24.Qxd4 removes the main attacker, defuses every check, and leaves a simpler rook endgame where I can try to set up a blockade.

White's Qxd4 took my queen, and my rook on d7 can simply recapture on d4 with nothing attacking that square (the f3 and c2 pawns don't cover it, and both white rooks are on b1/f1). After Rxd4 I'm up a bishop and knight for nothing in a dead-won rook endgame.

I'm down a bishop and knight, so I need material and activity: b7 is attacked by my rook and defended by nothing (Ra8 guards b8, not b7), so Rxb7 wins a clean pawn. I checked Black's counter-shots — Nxf3 is met by gxf3, and ...Rd1 just loses the rook to Rxd1 since no black piece covers d1.

I'm up a bishop and knight for a pawn, so I just need to grab material safely and keep everything defended — Bxa2 snatches the last loose pawn, and if 26.Rxf7 then Nxf7 simply nets a whole rook, while 26.Ra7 or 26.Rb8+ just drops the rook to Rxa7/Rxb8. The bishop on a2 isn't trapped since b1, b3, c4 and d5 are all available if the rook comes to a1.

I'm down two pieces, so I need activity plus any chance to win material back: Rb2 is safe (nothing — rook, knight, bishop or king — covers b2), it attacks the undefended bishop on a2, and it also shields my c2 pawn. I rejected Rd1/Rb4/Rd7 (all lose a rook outright to the undefended attack) and Rxf7 (Kxf7), and I don't want Rb8+ trading rooks when I'm the one needing counterplay.

I'm up a bishop and a knight, so the main thing is to rescue the attacked bishop on a2 without giving anything back. Bc4 steps out of the rook's reach while hitting the rook on f1, gaining a tempo, whereas Bb1/Bb3 just drop the piece and Nxf3 pointlessly trades material.

My rook on f1 is attacked by Bc4, so it must move, but 27.Rf2 loses to 27...Rd1+ 28.Rf1 Rxf1 mate (back rank!) and Rd1 drops a rook to Rxd1; among the safe squares I pick Re1 because it keeps the first rank guarded (any ...Rd1 is met by Rxd1), leaves c2 covered by Rb2, and immediately hits the completely undefended knight on e5. If Black answers 27...Nd3 then 28.cxd3 wins the piece back, and 27...Bd5 or any knight retreat lets me grab e5 or swing Rb6 against a6, which is my best practical try in a materially bad position.

I'm up a bishop and a knight for nothing, so my only job is to avoid tactics and consolidate — Nd3 looks like a fork but cxd3 just wins the knight, and Rd1 drops a rook to Rxd1. Rad8 doubles on the open d-file with no weaknesses, keeps Re8+ ideas covered, and prepares to invade on d1/d2 next.

I'm two pieces down, so my first duty is the back rank: any rook move or Rxe5 runs into ...Rd1+! 29.Re1 Rxe1+ which is mate since g2/h2 are blocked by my own pawns. 28.h3 gives my king the h2 escape square while keeping f3 defended by the g2 pawn and taking g4 from the knight, and it keeps my Re1 pressure on the undefended knight on e5 (with ...Nd3 still answered by cxd3).

I'm up a bishop and a knight, so simplification and safety matter most; Nd3 looks like a fork but cxd3 just wins the knight. Rd2 is completely safe (the c2 pawn blocks White's rook on b2 from reaching d2), it attacks c2, and it invites favorable rook trades.

Black's knight on e5 is completely undefended — Rd8 and Rd2 don't cover it, Bc4 doesn't either, and no pawn can recapture — so 29.Rxe5 wins a free piece and cuts my material deficit from two pieces to one. If Black answers Rd1+ I simply block with Rb1 and my king steps to h2 after the trade; if Rxc2 I trade rooks on c2 and head for a rook-plus-pawns defence.

I'm a full bishop up, so simplifying while grabbing another pawn is cleanest: Rxc2 forces Rxc2 Bxc2, leaving me rook+bishop+4 pawns against rook+3 pawns. I avoided Bd5 (Rxd5! Rxd5 Rxd2 loses material) and Rxg2 (Kxg2).

Black's rook on c2 is completely undefended — the bishop on c4 doesn't cover c2 and the d8 rook can't reach it — so Rxc2 simply wins a whole rook, leaving me rook-for-bishop up. After 30.Rxc2 Rd1+ 31.Kh2 there are no back-rank tricks, and my e5 rook and pawns are all safe.

My bishop on c4 is actually hanging to the rook on c2, so I must deal with that first — and Bd3 both rescues it and counterattacks the undefended rook on c2, winning a tempo. Keeping my rook on d8 is important: it means Re8+ is impossible (Rxe8 just wins a rook), and the rook also guards d3 along the file, so after something like Rc7 I can follow with f6 to kick the e5 rook.

My c2 rook is hanging to Bd3, so I must deal with it, and the best way is Rc3, which attacks the undefended bishop and gains a tempo while keeping both rooks (Rce2 or Rd5 would just lose a rook for the bishop). After Rc3 the bishop's squares are restricted — Bc4 and Be4 drop to Rxc4/fxe4, Bf5/Be2 to Rxf5/Rxe2 — so I keep my exchange-for-a-pawn advantage and can follow up with Rc7/Re7 doubling on the seventh.

My bishop on d3 is attacked by Rc3, and the ideal retreat is b5: from there it defends the a6 pawn, covers c6 and e8 (so Re8+ just loses a rook to Rxe8, and Rc6 drops to Bxc6), and it stays defended by the a6 pawn if White tries Rc5. Compared with Rd4 (which lets White invade with Re8+/Rcc8), Bb5 keeps my rook guarding the eighth rank while I aim to trade a pair of rooks into a drawish R vs B+pawn ending.

Rxb5 looks tempting but a6 recaptures, and trading a rook for bishop+pawn (or any rook trade like Re8+/Rc8) would leave only rook vs rook or rook vs bishop — throwing away my extra exchange, exactly the kind of mis-counted simplification my notes warn about. Instead I consolidate with the simplest useful move: Kh2 gives my king luft, kills all back-rank checks, and guards g2 against ...Rd2 ideas before I start hunting the a6 pawn with Rb3/Ra3.

I'm down a rook for a bishop, so my practical hope is to force a rook trade or grab counterplay; Rd2 puts the rook on the second rank hitting g2, and if White grabs with Rxb5 axb5 Rc2 Rxc2 I reach a pawn-up king-and-pawn ending. It also keeps the resource Bc4/Bd5 where my bishop is defended by the rook, inviting the exchange Rxd5 Rxd5 into an equal rook ending a pawn up.

I checked every destination against the b5-bishop's diagonals — Rc6, Rc4 and Re8+ all hang to the bishop, and Rxb5 axb5 Rxb5 just liquidates into a dead-equal rook ending, so those are out. Rc8+ is completely safe and forcing: f8/h8 are covered, ...Be8 and ...Rd8 both drop material to Rxe8+/Rxd8+, so Kh7 is forced and Black's king is pushed offside before I double on the seventh with Re7 and Rc7, where Black's only defence (...Rd7) lets me win the a6 or f7 pawn.

Both legal moves block the check but lose material: Rd8 drops the whole rook to Rxd8+, while Be8 only drops the bishop to Rxe8+. Losing the bishop and keeping my active rook on the second rank gives me far better practical chances, so I'll interpose the bishop.

The rook on c8 can capture the bishop on e8 with check along the eighth rank; f8 is covered by my other rook's support/the rook itself, and g7/h7 are blocked by Black's own pawns, with nothing able to capture or block on e8.

new_lessons: [middlegame] Before any quiet move, scan every enemy check; if a check (Qh4+/Qa5+ when f3 is played or king uncastled) wins the piece you just placed, choose differently Example: 11.Bc4?? Qh4+ 12.Bf2 Qxc4: f3/uncastled king made the e1-h4 check decisive, 55%→8%

[middlegame] List every enemy unit that can capture your destination square — pawn, piece, king — and play the move only if the recapture count favours you Example: ...Qc3 forked rooks but bxc3 took the queen; Ng5 died simply to hxg5

[middlegame] Count the entire capture sequence on a contested square; if stacked heavy pieces already hit your piece, trade or retreat it — adding a cheap defender feeds the sequence Example: 26.Ne5 and 27.Nhf3: Rxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 handed over two knights for one rook

[middlegame] When material ahead and a piece of yours is attacked, prefer offering an equal trade over a retreat that keeps tension; simplify toward a clearly won ending Example: 31.Rc3 (saving the rook actively) instead of 31.Rd5 trading into won R-vs-B: 94%→61%

[endgame] Rook plus pawns versus bishop plus pawns is a win — trade the last rooks happily; only bare rook versus bishop with no pawns is drawn Example: Refusing the rook trade "to keep the exchange" halved my winning chances in R+R vs R+B

[endgame] With extra material prefer the active move — rook to the seventh, attack weak pawns — over slow luft moves; play Kh2/h3 only against a concrete back-rank check Example: 32.Kh2 instead of 32.Rc7 gave Black time for ...g6 and a defensive setup

[middlegame] Each move name your undefended pieces and the squares (c2, d3, g4, your sixth/seventh rank) an enemy piece can enter; guard the loosest before starting anything active Example: Loose bishop plus loose pawn gave Black free tempi ...Nb4, ...d5, ...f5; rook then invaded d6-c6

[middlegame] Keep a knight or bishop on an advanced central square only if a pawn can support it; otherwise retreat before pawns chase it and it has no squares Example: Unsupported Ne4 had no safe retreat after e5/d6; Bd5 and Be4 were chased by pawns

[middlegame] Never push pawns in front of your king while an enemy bishop or queen eyes those squares; meet a wing pawn storm with a central break or file-opening capture Example: 17.g3 invited fxg3 and Bxh3; 17.dxc6 kept a winning game

[opening] When your bishop is attacked, pick the retreat that checks or gains a tempo and stops the opponent's planned central push, not the passive square Example: 6...Bb6 instead of Bb4+ allowed e5 and the d6 wedge; chances fell 50%→32%

[opening] When an enemy pawn wedges into your camp on the sixth or seventh rank, capture or blockade it at once; trades that leave it alive cost a piece Example: 10...Nxd2 ignored the d6 pawn; d6-d7xe7 then wrecked my structure

[opening] Before an exchange sequence on an open file, recount the defenders of your central pawns after every single trade, not just the first Example: 8.a4 axb5 axb5 Rxa8 removed e4's guard and lost the pawn to ...Nxe4

[endgame] Keep extra pawns connected and mutually defended; choose the recapture that keeps the chain linked even if it doubles a pawn Example: 29...dxc4 scattered a6/c4/c6 and Rd6-b6-a6 ate them; bxc4 held everything

[endgame] Before your king grabs material, count the pawn race and confirm your king stays inside the square of every enemy passer Example: 44...Kxh4 won a rook but f4-f5-f6 plus the h-pawn made two queens

[endgame] With queen versus lone king, never place the queen on a square touching that king unless your own king guards it; test Kxq and stalemate first Example: 66...Qc3+? Kxc3 threw away a won K+Q vs K and drew
